A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same nonlinear-Laplacian research. Their main text, equations, figures, references and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v2's new Appendix B.

before.justification: V1 reports original Gaussian planted-submatrix simulations, numerical optimization of nonlinearities, sensitivity analysis and transferability results in Figures 1–5.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds an explicit planted-clique comparison figure and a C. elegans network experiment in Appendix B.

M1.justification: Definition 1.5 extends the explicitly defined compressed algorithm from detection to recovery using Vv1(tilde L). Appendix B adds extraction of vertex subsets from the eigenvector's largest coordinates. The nonlinear-Laplacian construction and three approaches to tuning sigma remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix B adds dense-subgraph search on the 297-vertex C. elegans network, a limited extension to real graph data. Planted-clique numerical experiments were already mentioned in v1 Section 4.2; displaying them in v2 does not establish newly introduced coverage.

E2.justification: Direct spectral estimation remains the evaluated comparator, including in the added graph results. The compared nonlinearity families are retained. Correcting the discussion of cited AMP methods to BP does not introduce a newly evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix B introduces a protocol that makes the network binary and symmetric, selects 15 vertices using leading eigenvector coordinates, and measures the fraction of possible edges present. Existing synthetic-data and MLP settings are retained; Figure 5 uses the Figure 2 setup.

E4.justification: V2 adds a real-network applicability case study and compares the new theoretical eigenvector predictions with simulations in Figure 2. Figure 5 explicitly illustrates the planted-clique correspondence. The parameter-sensitivity and cross-distribution transferability analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 2 still reports averages over 500 inputs with plus/minus one standard deviation, and MLP optimization still uses 10 random initializations. Figure 5 adopts the existing uncertainty-reporting practice; no new statistical estimation or significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Appendix B newly reports 65% versus 73% edge density for 15-vertex subgraphs found by naive spectral and nonlinear-Laplacian methods. Figure 2 adds theoretical overlap predictions, and Figure 5 displays results identified as planted-clique validation, although one caption sentence inconsistently names the Gaussian model. Existing tuning thresholds and transferability values are retained.

T1.justification: Theorem 1.8 gains an explicit eigenvector-overlap limit, proved through eigenvalue differentiation and convexity in Section 3.5. Definition 1.1 relaxes subgaussianity to a finite third absolute moment and the sparsity lower bound from omega((log n)^c/n), c>6, to omega(log n/n). Sections 2.2 and 3.1–3.2 replace concentration and complex-analysis arguments with simpler convergence arguments. The unique-threshold guarantee is restricted to nonnegative signals.

C1.justification: V1 primarily guarantees detection and leaves recovery conjectural. V2's introductory Theorem 1.9 guarantees both strong detection and weak recovery for the compressed estimator when beta exceeds 0.76. The abstract and main theorem also qualify the earlier general claim of a unique signal-strength threshold.

C2.justification: V2 explains that general signed signal distributions may permit repeated appearance and disappearance of outliers. It qualifies BP/AMP efficiency and initialization comparisons and discusses applicability beyond the assumed random-matrix models in Appendix B. Existing dense-signal and compression limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A changes the code-access pointer from an anonymous repository to the named NonlinearLaplacian GitHub repository. Appendix B documents graph preprocessing and vertex selection. Existing architecture, training hyperparameters, hardware and runtime disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 1.7 adds connections to combined linear/spectral estimators, optimized phase-retrieval methods, robust AMP and large-scale eigenvector computation. It corrects the characterization of HWX17 and DM15 as dense BP rather than AMP. References supporting the new proof and network example are added, while some references tied to replaced arguments are removed.

P1.justification: V2 expands introductory motivation and related-work explanations, streamlines proof exposition, changes the eigenvector-analysis subsection from challenges to a proof, and adds Appendix B. The main section organization and most method and experimental prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 2 adds theoretical eigenvector markers and adjusts its vertical-axis presentation. A new Figure 5 displays the planted-clique comparison; the original transferability figure becomes Figure 6 without substantive display changes. Overall formatting is retained, although the new Figure 5 caption contains inconsistent model identification.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important theoretical gap: recovery was conjectural in v1, whereas Theorem 1.8 and Section 3.5 provide an explicit overlap formula and proof for the compressed estimator. Weaker assumptions and a corrected threshold scope further strengthen the central contribution. These gains outweigh limited reporting weaknesses in the added empirical material, particularly Figure 5's inconsistent caption and the sparsely specified real-network example.
